# Analysis

Looking at the training data, the highest Tc values (100-185 K) come from a few clear families:

**Top performers:**
- H2S1 → 185 K (special, hydride)
- Hg1Ba2Ca2Cu3O8 → 132 K
- Ba2Ca2Cu3O → 126 K
- Tl0.5Pb0.5Ba1.6Sr0.4Ca2Cu3O → 120 K
- Tl0.5Pb0.5Sr2Ca2Cu3... → 117 K
- Tl1Ba1Ca1Cu2O5.5 → 114 K
- Bi2Sr2Ca1Cu2O10 → 110 K
- Bi1.4Pb0.5Sb0.1Sr2Ca2Cu3O → 109 K
- Cu4.5V0.5Sr2Ca1O → 107 K
- Bi2Sr2Ca2Cu3O → 105.7 K

**Key insight:** Among the design variables provided (O, Cu, Ba, Sr, Y, Ca, La, Bi, Fe, Nb, C, Pr, As, B, Pb, Ce, Mo, V, Zn, Ni), the highest-Tc samples are dominated by the **cuprate family**: substantial O, Cu, and combinations of Ba/Sr/Ca, plus Bi, Pb, Tl (Tl not available).

The very best cuprates share these features:
- High **O** fraction (oxide backbone) — best examples have O near maximum
- Significant **Cu**
- Presence of **Ca** and **Sr/Ba** (the multi-layer "Ca-Cu-O" blocks give highest Tc)
- **Bi** and **Pb** appear in 105-120 K compounds
- Small amount of **V** appears in Cu4.5V0.5Sr2Ca1O (107 K)

**Design strategy:** Maximize the oxide-cuprate character. Push O to its max, keep Cu high, include Ca (which correlates with multilayer high-Tc phases), Ba+Sr, and add Bi+Pb (Bi-Pb-Sr-Ca-Cu-O reaches 109-110 K). Keep the pair-breaking/detrimental elements (Fe, Ni, Zn, Nb, Mo, As, B, C, Y, Pr, Ce) low, since Y-based cuprates cap ~93 K and Fe/Zn/Ni tend to suppress Tc in cuprates.

I'll set O, Cu, Ca, Ba, Sr, Bi, Pb high (within ranges), keep V small (mildly beneficial per Cu4.5V0.5 sample), and minimize the pair-breakers.

# Proposal
